title: The Truth About Talent (When Genes Matter and When They Don't)
coreMove: Match your habits to the temperament you already have instead of forcing the temperament the habit seems to require.

exampleSpecs.domain: a high-school cross-country coach deciding which event to enter a stocky, explosive freshman in after he keeps finishing mid-pack in the 5K
exampleSpecs.audience: a coach who has been told to develop every runner the same way
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the freshman quits the sport by spring or finds the 800m and stays four years
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the coach stops asking 'how do I make him a distance runner' and starts asking 'what is he already built to do that we can turn into a habit of training'

exampleSpecs.domain: a line cook with diagnosed ADHD trying to build a prep-list habit on a station where the head chef insists on a fixed written checklist
exampleSpecs.audience: a cook two years into the trade who keeps getting written up for skipped steps
exampleSpecs.stakes: keeping the job versus inventing a station layout that fits how his attention actually moves
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the cook redesigns the physical station so the next step is whatever is closest to his left hand, and the checklist becomes the room rather than the paper

exampleSpecs.domain: two siblings, one introverted and one extroverted, both trying to build a daily writing habit after reading the same productivity book
exampleSpecs.audience: a reader who suspects the advice that worked for a friend will not work for them
exampleSpecs.stakes: one sibling builds a four-year practice, the other burns out in eleven weeks, and the difference is not discipline
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the introvert builds the habit around silence and a closed door; the extrovert builds it around a standing coffee-shop appointment with a friend who also writes; neither approach is universal

exampleSpecs.domain: a pediatric nurse on night shift trying to keep a strength-training habit alive across a rotating schedule
exampleSpecs.audience: a shift worker who has read every habit book and noticed they all assume a 9-to-5
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether the habit survives the next schedule change or dies for the fourth time this year
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the nurse names the specific personality trait — high need for routine — that her schedule will never accommodate, and redesigns the habit to attach to sleep rather than time of day

exampleSpecs.domain: a tax accountant in his fifties who wants to learn jazz piano and keeps comparing himself to a colleague's daughter who started at six
exampleSpecs.audience: a late-starting adult learner with real but bounded talent
exampleSpecs.stakes: whether he keeps playing for the next thirty years or quits in shame within eight months
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: a teacher walks him through where genes have already set his ceiling, where they haven't, and what the next ten thousand hours actually buy at his age

exampleSpecs.domain: a regional sales manager choosing between two reps for a promotion: one a natural talker who hates paperwork, one a meticulous note-taker who freezes on cold calls
exampleSpecs.audience: a manager who has been promoting on charisma for a decade
exampleSpecs.stakes: a quarter-million-dollar territory and two careers
exampleSpecs.requiredBeat: the manager imagines designing the role around each rep's grain instead of grading them on the same rubric, and notices that 'best rep' is a question that cannot be answered without naming the territory
